ch08 - Introduction “Indiana Jones—I Always Knew Some Day You’d Come Walking Back through My Door. I Never Doubted Th.md
chapters.relation: Dean Kowalski's introduction uses the iconic theme music and Ford's underplaying of heroism to argue that Indy is expressive of the human condition: he loses fights, doesn't always choose wisely, and persists for decades despite unrequited love, estrangement from his father, and repeated failures. It poses the questions the volume pursues through the films — whether Indy should take a leap of faith about the supernatural events he witnesses, why artifacts belong in a museum, and what his 'fact, not truth' lecture (and the real Dr. Tyree 'right down the hall') means.

chapters.file: ch09 - Part I “It Was Wrong and You Knew It!” Ethics and Values.md
ch10 - 1 Acting Without Thinking The Sagacity of Indiana Jones.md
chapters.relation: Justin Kitchen rebuts the consequentialist charge (voiced by Big Bang Theory's Amy Farrah Fowler) that Indy plays no role in Raiders' outcome — the Nazis would have opened the Ark and died anyway — by shifting to virtue ethics: Indy's goodness lies in his character, not his consequences. His spontaneous 'I'm making this up as I go' decisions are read as Stoic sage-like action flowing from the two-stage moral education depicted in The Young Indiana Jones Chronicles, from Krishnamurti's lesson on death to Epictetus's 'winter training' in practice. The cardinal virtues as knowledge explain his instinctive courage (lifeboat, lead-lined refrigerator) and temperance (running past treasure), while his snake panic, his flash of greed at the Grail in Crusade, and his strained bonds with Marion and his father show he is a hero approaching but not yet attaining sagehood.

chapters.file: ch11 - 2 Does It Always Belong in a Museum.md
chapters.relation: Edwardo Pérez reconstructs the reasoning behind Indy's unargued mantra 'It belongs in a museum' via Bentham's principle of utility: museums maximize happiness because scholars and the public can study and enjoy artifacts for generations, unlike private collectors like Panama Hat. The same calculus explains his rule-breaking — he leaves the Mayapore Sankara Stone with the villagers ('It'd be another rock collecting dust' in a museum) because a flourishing village outweighs his fortune and glory, and he concedes the government's Area 51 warehouse may have been the utility-maximizing choice for the Ark after what it did to Belloq and Toht. Indy's apparent inconsistencies thus dissolve into case-by-case consequence weighing.

chapters.file: ch12 - 3 The Virtues that Made the Man, and the Man Who Became the Legend The Adventures in Philosophy of Young India.md
chapters.relation: Robert Mentyka reads The Adventures of Young Indiana Jones through Aristotle: Kazantzákis's causality lesson in 'Travels with Father' introduces the four causes, which the chapter applies to the TV series itself, and the final cause grounds ethics — eudaimonia is the ultimate end of all action, as young Indy learns when the Mata Hari affair in 'Demons of Deception' shows that pleasure cannot deliver fulfillment. Virtue is a mean between extremes (courage between cowardice and recklessness), acquired through vigilant practice and through community, illustrated by Indy swinging between caution and recklessness with Nancy Stratemeyer and Pancho Villa, and by exemplars like Albert Schweitzer and Ernest Hemingway. The 'adventures that made the man' were really the virtues and the people that shaped him, completed when Crusade and Crystal Skull have him accept his roles as son and father.

chapters.file: ch13 - 4 Raiders of the Lost Kant Indy Meets the Categorical Imperative.md
chapters.relation: Mia Wood tests Raiders against Kant's categorical imperative: Belloq's maxim of taking whatever he wants cannot be universalized without destroying property itself, and he repeatedly uses persons as mere means — deceiving the Hovitos about the Golden Idol, preying on Dietrich's fears, and treating Marion as a possession to be seduced with wine and a white dress. Indy fails too: his affair with the sixteen-year-old Marion ('It was wrong and you knew it'), leaving her bound and gagged to pursue the Ark, and Kant's absolutist ban on lying is probed through Katanga's noble lie to Dietrich. The first film's shadowy cinematography visualizes this moral ambiguity — Indy starts as merely one more 'raider' and only gradually redeems himself across the sequels.

chapters.file: ch14 - 5 Feminism and Indiana Jones A Field Guide.md
chapters.relation: Kate Schmidt applies feminist media tests (Bechdel, sexy lamp, Mako Mori, Pierce, Landau) to show the films usually fail — Willie is a screaming prop and human shield in Temple, the eyelid-writing student exists only to display Indy's sex appeal, and all four films fail the Bechdel Test — while Marion, Spalko, and above all Elsa in The Last Crusade are mixed cases with partial autonomy. Drawing on Iris Marion Young's account of women as Other and Carol Gilligan's care ethics, she argues Crusade is the series' most feminist film not for its women but for its men: Indy's open hurt after Elsa's betrayal and the father-son reconciliation embody care ethics against 'boys don't cry' toxic masculinity. She concludes that one can love flawed media without endorsing its sexism.

chapters.file: ch15 - Part II “…But Choose Wisely” Existentialism and Authenticity.md
ch16 - 6 The Absurd Hero Indiana Jones, God, and Sisyphus.md
chapters.relation: Justin Fetterman takes the Big Bang Theory objection seriously — Indy is superfluous in Raiders and loses nearly every artifact he chases — diagnosing him first with Kierkegaard's despair of possibility from The Sickness Unto Death, where each failure only convinces him success lies just ahead. But Indy refuses Kierkegaard's leap of faith even after witnessing Shiva's Sankara Stones and the Ark, since multiple gods' demonstrations cancel any single revelation, and Kierkegaard demands faith without comprehension. The chapter then re-reads him through Camus: like Sisyphus he repeats near-identical quests (Raiders and Crusade both have him lead the Nazis to a Judeo-Christian relic that destroys them), and his value lies in 'the most living' and the struggle itself, making him an absurd hero rather than a failed believer.

chapters.file: ch17 - 7 Indiana Jones and Existential Self-Affirmation.md
chapters.relation: Daniel Tilsley reads The Last Crusade as an excavation of identity: the fedora Fedora bestows after young Indy's defeat, the twenty-six-year quest for the Cross of Coronado ('All my life'), and the chosen name 'Indiana' (taken from the family dog) are acts of Nietzschean self-affirmation — amor fati and the willingness to will the Eternal Recurrence of one's life. The villains fail because they seek external artifacts to patch deficient lives, whereas the Grail Knight, like Camus's Sisyphus, authentically affirms his endless task of guarding the cup. The arc completes when Henry Sr. finally calls his son 'Indiana' while hanging from the abyss, recognizing the man he chose to become, and Crystal Skull repeats the pattern with Mutt and the fedora's eventual inheritance.

chapters.file: ch18 - 8 Nietzschean Themes in Raiders of the Lost Ark God May Be Dead, But Best Not Disturb His Corpse.md
chapters.relation: Duncan Gale reads Raiders through Nietzsche's Genealogy of Morals: the Nazis' contempt for those they exploit ('They hire only strong backs and they pay pennies') enacts master morality, while their ressentiment-driven project is itself a fatal misreading — both of the Ark and of Nietzsche, whom Walter Kaufmann shows was distorted by his anti-Semitic sister rather than responsible for it. Indy emerges as an overman candidate whose improvised self-legislation ('I'm making this up as I go,' casually shooting the scimitar-wielding warrior) creates life-affirming values, unlike Belloq, who has no code at all. The finale inverts the death of God: the Nazis die because they disturb a divine power they cannot harness, while America's de facto agnosticism — warehousing the Ark with 'top men' — proves the survivable response to nihilism.

chapters.file: ch19 - 9 Homeward Bound with Indiana Jones.md
chapters.relation: Charles Taliaferro and Annalissa Lane use Gabriel Marcel's creative fidelity — being 'at home' with oneself, others, and the sacred through availability ('avec') and presence rather than treating persons as furniture — to chart Indy's growth across all four films. Willie and Indy's vanity-driven near-tryst in Temple, the partnership of convenience with Marion in Raiders, the Zeppelin reckoning with Henry Sr. ('I was less important to you than people who had been dead for 500 years'), and the honest jeep argument about the broken engagement in Crystal Skull mark stages from self-deception toward being fully present to another. The church wedding closing Crystal Skull completes the journey into openness to the sacred, showing that home is a way of being rather than a place.

chapters.file: ch20 - Part III “Knowledge Was Their Treasure” Truth and Evidence.md
ch21 - 10 Fact, Truth, and Evidence A Lesson from Dr. Tyree.md
chapters.relation: Dean Kowalski stages an imagined dialogue between Indy and William E. Tyree — Harrison Ford's real Ripon College philosophy professor, whom Ford's own script rewrite placed 'right down the hall' — to show that 'archaeology is the search for fact, not truth' is self-defeating if truth is correspondence with reality. Tyree's epistemology primer (principles of evidence, inductive generalization, hypothesis testing like Indy's Sankara-stone glow prediction, and Ockham's Razor) explains Indy's resistance to the God hypothesis despite witnessing the Ark, the Grail's instant healing of Henry Sr., and the invisible bridge he crossed on guesswork rather than knowledge. The resolution: Indy practices methodological naturalism, keeping deeper truths out of archaeology, without being committed to metaphysical naturalism.

chapters.file: ch22 - 11 Indiana Jones and the Quest for Agnosticism What if All Stories Are True.md
chapters.relation: Robert Grant Price observes that in Indy's world every myth — the Ark, the Sankara Stones, the Grail, and in the comics and novels Atlantis, Merlin, Noah's Ark, and the Philosopher's Stone — turns out factually true, producing a surplus of evidence for mutually exclusive religions (the personal Christian Trinity versus non-personal Brahman). Against Derrida's deconstruction and the postmodern claim that no grand narrative captures truth, in Indy's world 'the squash ball always comes back' — yet he stays agnostic, telling Spalko 'There is always another explanation.' The chapter weighs his three exits: remain agnostic, take a leap of faith as he does stepping onto the invisible bridge, or read Percival and Galahad as symbolically rather than historically true.

chapters.file: ch23 - 12 The Shadow Realities of Indiana Jones.md
chapters.relation: Matthew Crippen and Matthew Dixon read the franchise's caves through Plato's allegory: in Crusade, stand-ins for God (the Cross of Coronado, the Grail, with the decoy chalices as shadows of a representation) appear underground, while Indy's self-realizations with his father occur at sunlit cave mouths, inching from shadow toward the Good. They fuse this with newer, active accounts of truth — James's 'truth happens to an idea' realized in the leap from the lion's head, Dewey on poetry as revelation, and Heidegger's aletheia as unconcealment — while Nietzsche's critique shows Platonic fictions can still be life-enhancing. The father and son 'shadow' one another (with Oedipal overtones through Elsa) until Henry Sr. relinquishes the Grail to save 'Indiana,' his path out of the cave.

holes.name: Nihilism
holes.what: The diagnosis that the collapse of God-grounded absolute values leaves life apparently meaningless — which Nietzsche warned against rather than endorsed.
holes.why: Chapter 18 frames Raiders' Nazis and Belloq as failing through the wrong reaction to nihilism and Indy's improvised values as overcoming it, but taxonomy has no nihilism slug.

holes.name: Gabriel Marcel
holes.what: French Christian existentialist (1889–1973) whose 'creative fidelity' analyzes commitment, availability ('être avec'), presence versus objectification, and openness to the sacred.
holes.why: Chapter 19's entire reading of Indy's path home across all four films is built on Marcel's creative fidelity and 'being at home,' and Marcel is absent from taxonomy.

holes.name: Methodological vs Metaphysical Naturalism
holes.what: The distinction between doing science while bracketing the supernatural (methodological naturalism) and denying that anything supernatural exists at all (metaphysical naturalism).
holes.why: Chapter 21 resolves Indy's 'fact, not truth' stance as methodological naturalism, its central interpretive distinction, which taxonomy lacks.

holes.name: Correspondence Theory of Truth
holes.what: The view that a statement is true when it accurately describes how things actually are, facts being the features of reality that make statements true.
holes.why: Chapter 21's opening argument that 'archaeology seeks fact, not truth' is self-defeating rests entirely on this account of truth, which taxonomy lacks.

holes.name: Agnosticism
holes.what: T. H. Huxley's position that reason and evidence do not suffice to justify either belief or disbelief in God, suspending judgment between theism and atheism.
holes.why: Chapter 22 argues Indy's surplus of confirming evidence for rival religions lands him in exactly this agnosticism ('There is always another explanation'), which taxonomy lacks.

holes.name: Joseph Campbell
holes.what: Comparative mythologist (1904–1987) who argued that cross-cultural myths share archetypes, notably the hero's journey, springing from primal human realities.
holes.why: Chapter 23 credits Campbell (Lucas's inspiration) for the cave-as-archetype frame and closes by saying Crusade deals with 'ideas percolating in the collective culture that Campbell described,' yet taxonomy lacks him.
